tldr: Incorporating human organization theory principles—specifically pooled and sequential interdependence—the authors propose ORCH, a framework that dynamically organizes heterogeneous robot teams of up to 50 agents into task-specific hierarchies. ORCH significantly outperforms prior methods in task completion score and execution efficiency across wildfire-response missions, demonstrating that collective intelligence relies heavily on organizational structure rather than mere model scale.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of ORCH. (A) A hierarchical organization is constructed from the task description and available robots, either by human experts or an LLM with a Critic. (B) A closed-loop execution loop runs bi-directional communication every step: bottom-up reporting and top-down instruction. (C) Horizontal managers handle concurrent work (pooled interdependence), and (D) vertical managers handle phase-ordered work (sequential interdependence). Together, they enable (E) large-scale coordination of heterogeneous robots in complex wildfire environments.
overview:
When deploying multiple robots or AI agents to tackle complex real-world tasks, prior approaches have typically relied on fixed organizational structures—such as flat peer-to-peer communication among all agents or a single central manager directing everyone. However, when teams scale up to 50 agents and combine diverse robot types (drones, helicopters, firefighters, bulldozers), these rigid setups break down. A single manager's context window and cognitive load become saturated, while all-to-all communication drowns the system in noise and network delays.

To solve this, the authors turned to human organization theory. In human organizations, roles and coordination mechanisms are split based on task structure: work that can be carried out concurrently in parallel (pooled interdependence) is handled differently from work where one step strictly depends on completing a prior step (sequential interdependence). Inspired by this principle, the authors developed ORCH (Organizing Roles and Coordination Hierarchies), a framework that constructs flexible organizational structures tailored to the task and available resources. By recursively combining horizontal managers (coordinating concurrent operations) and vertical managers (governing temporal phase transitions), ORCH organizes context-appropriate "teams of teams" either through human design or automated LLM generation.

To evaluate the system, the authors substantially expanded the dynamically spreading wildfire simulator CREW-Wildfire into 25 diverse missions, testing teams of up to 50 agents powered by eight state-of-the-art LLMs. ORCH consistently outperformed four representative embodied multi-agent frameworks, dramatically boosting task score and execution efficiency. Remarkably, the results also revealed that collective intelligence is not monotonically determined by raw LLM parameter scale, but is strongly governed by well-designed organizational structure.
contributions: Engineered human organization theory (pooled and sequential interdependence) into embodied AI, establishing the ORCH framework to seamlessly manage both concurrent and order-dependent work.

Implemented a closed-loop execution mechanism that dynamically builds task-specific organizational hierarchies and adapts to dynamic environments via per-step bi-directional communication (bottom-up progress reporting and top-down plan revision).

Demonstrated substantial improvements in mission score and execution efficiency over prior methods through extensive evaluations across 25 wildfire-response missions, up to 50 heterogeneous robots, and eight modern LLMs.

Showed that collective multi-agent performance does not scale monotonically with LLM model size, highlighting organizational design as an independent and fundamental variable for collective intelligence.

sections.heading: From Individual Intelligence to Collective Intelligence: Why Organization Matters
sections.summary: No matter how capable individual agents or robots are, a team cannot realize its full collective potential without an organizational structure tailored to the task. This section outlines the motivation behind ORCH, which adapts the management of task interdependencies from human organization theory into embodied AI.
sections.details:
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and reinforcement learning have equipped individual agents with impressive reasoning and long-horizon execution skills. However, grouping multiple agents into effective teams remains an open challenge. As team size grows, coordination costs explode—deciding who communicates with whom, who takes on which role, and how actions are timed becomes overwhelmingly complex.

Most prior multi-agent studies have relied on fixed organizational structures, such as decentralized setups where all agents talk equally or centralized setups where one leader directs everyone. However, communication needs differ fundamentally between independent parallel searches across separate areas and strict sequential workflows—for example, where a drone must spot a fire first, a helicopter must airlift firefighters and water supplies next, and ground crews must then build containment lines.

In human societies, as detailed in organization theory pioneered by James D. Thompson, work interdependencies are broadly categorized into two types:
- Pooled Interdependence: Members work independently to contribute to a shared objective in parallel (e.g., distributed multi-agent reconnaissance or obstacle removal).
- Sequential Interdependence: The output of one task serves as the prerequisite input for the next (e.g., dispatching fire suppression teams only after the fire origin is located).

This distinction is the core insight of the paper. The research began with a key question: Can dynamically structuring organizational topology based on task interdependencies unlock high collective intelligence in large, heterogeneous robot teams?

sections.heading: The Challenge of Scaling Collectives and a Wildfire Testbed
sections.summary: The authors examine why coordinating large, long-horizon real-world tasks is so difficult, and introduce their extended wildfire benchmark, CREW-Wildfire. Spanning 25 missions with dynamic fire propagation, communication cutoffs, and sudden victim discoveries, it rigorously tests flexible organizational adaptation.
sections.details:
### Hurdles in Organizing Agent Collectives
In flat organizations where every agent talks to everyone else, communication volume scales quadratically ($O(N^2)$), causing global decision-making to collapse. Conversely, in single-manager architectures, adding more robots quickly overflows the manager LLM's context window and decision-making capacity, leaving it unable to handle dynamic replanning. A multi-tier organization is therefore essential: one that aggregates local situations while breaking global objectives down into manageable sub-goals.

### A Demanding Testbed: Extended CREW-Wildfire
To test the efficacy of organizational structures, the authors heavily extended the wildfire response simulator CREW-Wildfire. Key features include:
- Cellular Automata-based Realistic Fire Spread: Wildfire propagation shifts dynamically based on terrain slope, wind speed and direction, vegetation type, and soil moisture. Initial reconnaissance data quickly becomes obsolete, penalizing rigid static plans and demanding rapid dynamic adaptation.
- Four Heterogeneous Agent Types: Specialized reconnaissance "Drones", long-distance transit and airlift "Helicopters", clearing-specialized "Bulldozers", and versatile "Firefighters" capable of clearing, rescue, and suppression.
- 25 Diverse Missions: Spanning simple clearing tasks with 3 agents up to large-scale joint operations with 50 agents. Missions also feature unexpected events such as drone hardware failures, newly spotted victims, and sudden fire flare-ups.

sections.heading: The ORCH Architecture: Two Manager Types and Closed-Loop Communication
sections.summary: This section details the core design of ORCH: a tree-structured hierarchy combining horizontal managers for concurrent work and vertical managers for sequential work, supported by a step-by-step bi-directional communication protocol.
sections.details:
### Constructing Task-Specific Hierarchies
Given a task description $T$, available robots $W$, and their capabilities $C$, ORCH generates a tree-structured organizational hierarchy $G$ (formulated as $G = H(T, W, C)$). Leaf nodes represent the physical robots, while intermediate nodes act as managers. Hierarchies can be created in two ways: designed by human experts, or automatically generated by an LLM paired with a Critic. In the automated pipeline, an LLM drafts an organizational proposal, and a separate Critic model iteratively inspects and refines it by checking for superfluous tiers and capability-role mismatches.

### Hybrid Arrangement of Horizontal and Vertical Managers
Grounded in organization theory, ORCH recursively pairs two distinct manager types:
- Horizontal Managers (Pooled Interdependence): Handle tasks that can proceed concurrently. They distribute subtasks $t_i$ across subordinate agents $\mathcal{C}$ while preventing duplicated effort (formulated as $\mathcal{T}_h = f_h(M, P, R)$, where $M$ is the goal, $P$ is estimated progress, and $R$ is subordinate feedback).
- Vertical Managers (Sequential Interdependence): Manage order-dependent workflows. They decompose the mission into a sequence of temporal phases $\Phi = \{\phi_1, \dots, \phi_K\}$, activating and assigning only the tasks required for the active phase $\phi_k$ (formulated as $\mathcal{T}_v^{(k)} = f_v(\phi_k, M, P_m, P_p, R)$). When completion conditions are met, the manager advances the team to the next phase.

Combining these allows for a flexible multi-tier "team of teams": vertical managers orchestrate high-level mission phases (Reconnaissance $\rightarrow$ Transport $\rightarrow$ Suppression), while nested horizontal managers supervise concurrent operations within each phase (such as distributed sector-by-sector searching).

### Bi-Directional Hierarchical Communication Protocol
At each simulation time step, the organization executes two alternating phases:
- Bottom-Up Reporting Phase: Physical worker robots inspect their observations and submit structured reports containing task completion status, progress estimates, and urgent alerts to their parent managers. Managers summarize these reports and pass them up the chain.
- Top-Down Planning Phase: Decisions flow downward from the root manager. Subordinates provide feedback on whether assigned instructions are feasible given their current state; if not, the manager adjusts the plan. Once agreed upon, worker robots translate the tasks into low-level actions and execute them simultaneously.

Depicting (A) hierarchy generation, (B) the closed-loop bi-directional execution loop, (C) horizontal managers handling concurrent distributed exploration, (D) vertical managers governing sequential phased suppression, and (E) their integrated execution in a 50-agent wildfire containment mission.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Substantial Gains from Organization and an Inverted Scaling Trend
sections.summary: Evaluated across 25 missions and 8 LLMs, ORCH consistently outperformed four baseline frameworks. The results demonstrate that human-designed structures yield top performance, Critic modules are critical for organization quality, and raw LLM model size does not directly dictate collective team performance.
sections.details:
### Decisive Coordination Gains over Baselines
ORCH was benchmarked against four representative embodied multi-agent frameworks: CAMON (dynamic leader election), COELA (modular cognitive architecture), HMAS-2 (hybrid centralized-decentralized), and Embodied (prompt-prescribed organizational structures).
The improvements were striking. Compared to the average of the four baselines, human-designed ORCH improved the final mission score by 63.97% and execution efficiency (AUC of the progress curve) by 74.29%. Even automatically generated ORCH hierarchies achieved 43.63% and 52.53% improvements, respectively (Fig. F2 A). In overall win-rate rankings across all tasks, LLMs, and seeds, human-designed ORCH took first place at 32.6%, followed by automated ORCH at 26.2%, far outpacing prior methods (Fig. F2 B). Two-way ANOVA confirmed that the main effect of the algorithm was highly significant ($p < 0.01$), whereas the interaction effect between algorithm and LLM backbone was not significant ($p = 0.62$). This confirms that ORCH's advantage stems from its organizational structure, not accidental synergy with a specific LLM.

### Model Size Does Not Monotonically Determine Collective Performance
Evaluating eight LLM backbones (including ChatGPT-5.4, Gemma-4-it, Qwen-3.6, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro) revealed a surprising inversion. Mid-sized models like Gemma-4-it and Qwen-3.6 achieved higher collective team performance under ORCH than frontier flagship models like ChatGPT-5.4 or DeepSeek-V4-Pro, despite the latter leading coding and math benchmarks (Fig. F3). In collective coordination, adherence to assigned roles, succinct and accurate status reporting, and reliable translation of upstream commands into physical actions prove far more critical than raw standalone reasoning capability.

### Large-Scale 50-Agent Mission Dynamics and Ablation Findings
In the most challenging "Scale Level Complex" mission (25 firefighters, 10 drones, 10 helicopters, and 5 bulldozers), vertical managers maintained four distinct phases: (1) Reconnaissance $\rightarrow$ (2) Fire Monitoring & Route Clearance $\rightarrow$ (3) Water Supply & Troop Deployment $\rightarrow$ (4) Fireline Construction & Suppression. Subordinate horizontal managers simultaneously coordinated parallel actions within each phase, achieving seamless team-wide synchronization.

Ablation analyses on organizational generation (Figs. F4 A, B and F5) revealed:
- Human-designed organizations were the shallowest and most balanced (mean tree depth 1.20, span-of-control variance 1.48).
- LLM generation without a Critic introduced redundant middle-management tiers and excessive depth (mean depth 1.56, average managers 2.08), resulting in communication delays, decision confusion, and degraded performance.
- Communication failure analysis (Fig. F4 C) showed that while baselines failed primarily due to leaf-node execution failures (51.2%–64.5%), ORCH slashed execution failure rates down to 13.1%–20.7%. Proper hierarchical filtering ensures leaf workers receive actionable, feasible assignments.

captions.F2: Performance comparison across all 25 missions and 8 LLMs. (A) Progress curves and radar charts show human-designed and LLM-generated ORCH outperforming baselines in score, execution efficiency, and token usage. (B) Win-rate distributions and (C) ANOVA results further highlight ORCH's robust and consistent advantage.
captions.F3: Collective performance broken down by LLM backbone. Across both human-designed (A) and LLM-generated (B) hierarchies, mid-sized models such as Gemma-4-it and Qwen-3.6 outperform massive flagship models, demonstrating an inverted scaling trend in multi-agent collaboration.
captions.F4: Organizational structure analysis and ablations. (A) Performance impact with vs. without a Critic, (B) comparison of tree depth and span-of-control variance, and (C) failure mode categorization from communication logs showing ORCH dramatically reduces worker execution failures.
captions.F5: Comparison of generated organizational charts in the 50-agent complex mission. Human experts build clean, role-specialized teams, whereas raw LLMs introduce bloated hierarchies. Adding a Critic prunes unnecessary managers and produces streamlined structures.

sections.heading: Summary and Outlook: A New Frontier in Artificial Collective Intelligence
sections.summary: This section synthesizes the core takeaways, emphasizing the central role of organizational design in embodied AI. It also discusses existing limitations, such as dynamic in-mission restructuring and support for other interdependence types, outlining promising directions for future work.
sections.details:
The primary takeaway of this work is clear: advancing collective intelligence is not just about making individual agents smarter—how those agents are organized is a decisive factor. By operationalizing classic human organization principles (pooled and sequential interdependence), ORCH enables up to 50 heterogeneous robots to coordinate smoothly while adapting to rapidly shifting environments.

Nevertheless, the authors candidly highlight several limitations and open challenges:
- Dynamic Organizational Restructuring: In the current version of ORCH, the hierarchy's tree topology is fixed at initialization; it does not dynamically alter the organization chart itself (e.g., restructuring or spinning off new sub-units) midway through execution.
- Modeling Broader Forms of Interdependence: The framework currently focuses on pooled and sequential workflows. Human organizations also exhibit reciprocal interdependence, where members continuously adjust back-and-forth in real time, requiring new manager primitives.
- Gap in Human vs. LLM Organization Design: While introducing a Critic elevates automated LLM hierarchy generation to practical performance, human-crafted organizations remain more compact and effective. Further research is needed for LLMs to master organizational design autonomously.

As robot teams become larger and tackle increasingly open-ended missions, organizational theory will likely emerge as an essential pillar of collective AI, on par with model architectures and planning algorithms.

takeaways: Coordination bottlenecks caused by scaling the number and diversity of robots can be dramatically relieved by hierarchical organizations that separate parallel work (horizontal) from sequential work (vertical).
Collective multi-agent performance depends more on organizational aptitude—such as strict role adherence and concise reporting—than on raw LLM parameter scale.
When prompting LLMs to design team organizational charts, pairing them with a Critic agent is essential to prevent bloated, inefficient middle-management hierarchies.
Multi-agent embodied AI is experiencing a paradigm shift, moving from the sole pursuit of individual agent capability to the systematic optimization of organizational structure.
limitations: The hierarchical tree structure is established prior to mission start; dynamic runtime restructuring (such as mid-mission rescaling or re-organization) is not yet supported.
Interdependence modeling is restricted to pooled and sequential types; handling reciprocal interdependence, which requires continuous real-time mutual adjustments among agents, remains future work.
Standalone LLM hierarchy generation remains prone to redundancy compared to human expert design, leaving a performance gap in automated organizational design.
Evaluations are currently limited to the simulated wildfire domain (CREW-Wildfire); real-world robotic deployment and cross-domain generalizability require further validation.
